candidates.headline: Players found 'made with suno' inside the music files of a Binding of Isaac update, and the songs were pulled
candidates.what_happened: A Repentance+ update for The Binding of Isaac added a GTA-themed daily run with 14 new music files. A Reddit user ran the files through ffprobe and found Suno's own tag, with a creation time of 30 October 2026, in the metadata of some tracks, and none of this was disclosed on Steam. Nicalis pushed an emergency update removing the music on about 21 November, after recent Steam reviews fell to about 9% positive.
candidates.named_thing: The metadata line in drivingsong1.ogg: "made with suno; created=2026-10-30T17:53:41Z"

primary.label: Kotaku, Ethan Gach, 'Binding Of Isaac Update Review-Bombed Over AI-Generated Music In GTA 6 Mode', 21 Nov 2026
primary.quote: comment : made with suno; created=2026-10-30T17:53:41Z; id=cd5a5b55-bead-4cb9-949d-09ed1f917dce

second.label: Nintendo Life, Jim Norman, 'Binding Of Isaac Dev Shocked To Find GenAI Music In Repentance+', Nov 2026 (page shows Mon, likely 23 Nov)
second.quote: mentions of the AI music 'tool' Suno in select tracks' metadata

more_sources.label: Kotaku, same article, on the file count
more_sources.quote: The new update includes 14 music files for the run; seven full songs, plus some derivatives (intros/outros),

more_sources.label: Kotaku, same article, on the fix
more_sources.quote: An emergency update has since gone out to remove the AI-generated music

more_sources.label: Fortune, Catherina Gioino, on GTA VI itself, 25 Nov 2026 (context only)
more_sources.quote: generative AI has zero part in what Rockstar Games is building.

candidates.money_or_mechanism: The teardown is literal: a free command-line tool read the tags Suno writes into every file it exports, so the build was visible to any player, and some files had the tag scrubbed because they were edited and exported again.
candidates.why_it_matters: A game studio that buys or makes AI music without saying so can be caught by its own file metadata, and the cost lands on the game's reviews.
candidates.funny: The game's tribute to Grand Theft Auto used AI music; the real Grand Theft Auto VI, out the same week, was made with none.
candidates.risks: Event date is from Kotaku's 21 Nov story; the update itself went out a day or so earlier. Who put the music in is disputed: McMillen says it was Nicalis's idea and Nicalis has not explained. The Verge's story (22 Nov) could not be fetched. Nintendo Life shows no full date.

candidates.headline: The New York Times folded its newsroom AI agents into one tool, News Agent, and reporters must pass legal training to use it
candidates.what_happened: On 24 November 2026 Ulrike Langer's News Machines described News Agent, the New York Times' internal tool that combines archive search across 175 years of the paper, stylebook checks, Freedom of Information Act drafting and document analysis. Journalists get access only after legal standards training, and the Times will not say which AI models run it. Its forerunner, the Epstein Files Engine, turned reporters' questions into BigQuery SQL and was asked about 4,500 questions by more than 100 journalists, contributing to at least 20 stories.

candidates.money_or_mechanism: The build is a set of agents over the paper's own archive and stylebook, with a language model writing database queries and returning citations a reporter can check, and a legal training gate in front of it.

candidates.headline: Prime Video built an AI model that flags every pass and carry that moves the ball forward in Champions League games
candidates.what_happened: On 23 November 2026 Prime Video announced Progressive Actions, a Prime Insight on its Prime Vision feed for UEFA Champions League games, debuting at Arsenal against Borussia Dortmund on 24 November in the UK and Ireland, and also in Germany and Italy. Its own AI models measure how far the ball travels in each phase of the pitch, with a shorter threshold near the opposition goal, then show the start, end, player and distance live. It was built by Prime Video's producers, engineers, AI specialists and on-air analysts.

candidates.headline: HeyGen says its new avatar is 84.4% indistinguishable from real video; its own test shows viewers picked it as real 42.2% of the time
candidates.what_happened: HeyGen released Avatar 6 on 17 November 2026, a model that turns a photo or a short clip plus an audio track into a talking video at 1080p or 2K, with gestures cued from the script. Its research page explains the headline number: shown real footage and Avatar 6 side by side, raters picked Avatar 6 as the real one 42.2% of the time across 270 answers, which HeyGen scores as 84.4% of the way to a coin toss. Shown one clip at a time, 65.1% of Avatar 6 clips were judged real against 78.9% for real recordings.

candidates.headline: Google opened Genie 4, a model that streams playable worlds at 24 frames a second, to developers at about 10 cents a second
candidates.what_happened: On 19 November 2026 Google made Genie 4 available to developers through the Gemini API and AI Studio. It generates a continuous 720p world at 24 frames a second with sound, seeded by text or an image and steered live with the keyboard and text prompts, with each frame generated as the session runs. Its documentation prices it at roughly $0.10 per second of streamed output, and sessions run for up to 120 seconds.

primary.label: Google, The Keyword, 'Genie 4 in the Gemini API', 19 Nov 2026
primary.quote: generating continuous 720p worlds at 24fps with synchronized native audio

second.label: PPC Land, 'Google charges developers about 10 cents a second for Genie 4 worlds', 19 Nov 2026
second.quote: Each session can run for up to 120 seconds.

more_sources.label: Google, same post, on availability
more_sources.quote: Genie 4 is now available for developers through the Gemini API.

more_sources.label: PPC Land, same article, on price

more_sources.label: PPC Land, same article, on how frames are made
more_sources.quote: Each frame is generated by the model as the session runs.

candidates.money_or_mechanism: There is no game engine underneath: every frame is a model's guess at the next one, billed by the second, which is why a session stops at two minutes and Google lists long-term scene permanence as an open problem.
candidates.why_it_matters: Game makers pricing a prototype can see what a generated world costs per minute of play and how long it holds together.
candidates.funny: An hour of your generated game costs about $360 to stream, and it can only remember the last two minutes.
candidates.risks: Weakest on the beat: a general AI lab launch, and Google's post names prototyping, spatial visualisation and robotics, not game studios; no game studio using it in the window was found. The $360 an hour is my arithmetic from $0.10 a second, and 120 seconds is the session cap, not a memory measure; check the joke against those exact facts. The image is a small Project Genie thumbnail.

candidates.headline: Epic used AI to rewrite more than 20,000 Fortnite Blueprints as about 3 million lines of Verse, then dropped Blueprints from Unreal Engine 6
candidates.what_happened: In an update reported on 20 and 21 November 2026, Epic said an AI-assisted run had converted more than 20,000 of Fortnite Battle Royale's visual Blueprints into a working prototype written in its Verse language, about 3 million lines, a job it had expected to take years. On that basis Unreal Engine 6, Early Access included, will ship without Blueprints or the Actor gameplay framework, reversing its June 2026 roadmap. Epic says the team is still checking the generated code's performance, memory and architecture.
